title: A phone call about an interview
lines: Hello, is that Daniel Ruiz? This is Maria from Greenline Solar.
We received your CV for the technician job, and we'd like to invite you for an interview.
Oh, that's great news. When is it?
Is Thursday at eleven o'clock OK for you?
Thursday is difficult, because I work in the morning. Is Friday possible?
Yes, Friday at eleven is fine. Please bring a copy of your driving licence and your certificates.
No problem. Where exactly is the office?
We're on the second floor of the building next to the train station. Ask for me at reception.
Perfect. Thank you very much, Maria. See you on Friday.

q.q: Why does the woman call the man?
q.a: To invite him to an interview for the technician job.

q.q: Why can't he go on Thursday?
q.a: Because he works in the morning.

q.q: What must he bring to the interview?
q.a: A copy of his driving licence and his certificates.

q.q: Where is the office?
q.a: On the second floor of the building next to the train station.

gaps.s: We received your ___ for the technician job.
Thursday is difficult, because I work in the ___.
We're on the second floor of the building next to the train ___.

title: After the interview
lines: Hi, Laura! I've just finished my interview.
Hi, Tom! How did it go?
I think it went well. There were two people, a manager and a woman from human resources.
They asked why I wanted to change jobs, and what I know about their company.
I said I want more responsibility. Luckily, I read about the company on their website last night.
Well done. Did they say anything about money?
Yes, the salary is a bit higher than now, and there are twenty-five days of holiday.
That sounds really good. When will you know?
They'll call me next week. I'm trying not to think about it!

q.q: How many people interviewed the man, and who were they?
q.a: Two: a manager and a woman from human resources.

q.q: Why does he want to change jobs?
q.a: Because he wants more responsibility.

q.q: How did he prepare for the question about the company?
q.a: He read about the company on their website the night before.

q.q: When will he get an answer?
q.a: Next week, by phone.

gaps.s: I've just finished my ___.
Luckily, I read about the company on their ___ last night.
They'll call me next ___.

title: Questions at the end
lines: So, Mark, that's all from me. Do you have any questions for us?
Yes, I have a few. What does a normal day look like in this job?
Well, in the morning you visit clients, and in the afternoon you write reports in the office.
Will I have a company car?
Yes, you will. And we pay for your phone too.
Great. Is there any training at the beginning?
Yes. For the first two weeks you'll work with an experienced colleague.
That's really useful. And when would the job start?
At the beginning of next month. We'll tell you our decision by Wednesday.
Thank you for your time. It was nice to meet you.

q.q: What does a normal day in the job look like?
q.a: Visiting clients in the morning and writing reports in the office in the afternoon.

q.q: What does the company give the employee, apart from the salary?
q.a: A company car and they pay for his phone.

q.q: What happens in the first two weeks?
q.a: He works with an experienced colleague.

q.q: When will they tell him their decision?
q.a: By Wednesday.

gaps.s: Do you have any ___ for us?
In the afternoon you write ___ in the office.
For the first two weeks you'll work with an experienced ___.

title: Explaining a gap in your CV
lines: I notice there's a gap of about a year in your CV. Could you tell me about that?
Of course. After my company closed, I decided to take some time to retrain. I did a course in renewable energy installations.
It was part-time, so I also worked in my uncle's business, mostly helping with electrical repairs.
I see. And why renewable energy, specifically?
Honestly, I could see that most new projects in the region were solar or wind, and I didn't want to be left behind.
That makes sense. How have you applied what you learned?
Last spring I helped design a small solar installation for a farm. It's now producing around forty per cent of their electricity.
That's impressive. Did you have any problems with the project?
The roof was weaker than we expected, so we had to change the mounting system. It delayed us by two weeks, but the client was happy in the end.

q.q: Why is there a gap in the man's CV?
q.a: His company closed and he took time to retrain with a course in renewable energy installations.

q.q: What else did he do during that year?
q.a: He worked part-time in his uncle's business, mostly on electrical repairs.

q.q: Why did he choose renewable energy?
q.a: Because most new projects in the region were solar or wind and he didn't want to be left behind.

q.q: What problem did the farm project have, and what was the result?
q.a: The roof was weaker than expected, so they changed the mounting system; it was delayed by two weeks but the client was happy.

gaps.s: I decided to take some time to ___.
I didn't want to be left ___.
The roof was ___ than we expected.

title: Talking about salary
lines: Before we finish, I'd like to talk about your salary expectations.
Sure. Based on my research, similar positions in the area pay between thirty-two and thirty-six thousand.
Our budget for this role is closer to thirty thousand, I'm afraid.
I understand. Is there any flexibility, considering that I already have experience with the software you use?
There might be a little. We could start at thirty-one and review it after the probation period.
How long is the probation period?
Six months. If everything goes well, you'd also receive an annual bonus.
What would the bonus depend on?
Mainly on the team's results, and on your own objectives, which we'd agree together.
That sounds fair. Could you send me the details in writing so I can think about it?
Of course. You'll have an email by tomorrow.

q.q: What salary range does the man mention, and how did he get it?
q.a: Between thirty-two and thirty-six thousand, based on his research on similar positions in the area.

q.q: What argument does he use to ask for more money?
q.a: That he already has experience with the software the company uses.

q.q: What does the woman finally offer?
q.a: To start at thirty-one thousand and review it after the six-month probation period, plus an annual bonus.

q.q: What does the man ask for at the end?
q.a: For the details in writing so he can think about it.

gaps.s: I'd like to talk about your salary ___.
Is there any ___, considering that I already have experience?
If everything goes well, you'd also receive an annual ___.

title: A video interview goes wrong
lines: Hello? Can you hear me? I think my camera isn't working.
I can hear you, but I can't see you. Try turning the video off and on again.
Yes, perfect. Don't worry, it happens all the time. Shall we start?
Yes, sorry about that. I tested everything this morning.
No problem at all. So, tell me why you applied for a job that's mostly remote.
I've worked from home for two years, so I know how to organise myself. And I'd save almost two hours of commuting every day.
How do you stay in touch with your team when you're not in the office?
We have a short video call every morning, and we use a chat app for quick questions. I also try to meet colleagues in person once a month.
That's a good habit. Remote work can feel lonely sometimes.

q.q: What technical problem does the man have at the start?
q.a: His camera isn't working, so she can hear him but can't see him.

q.q: How does she suggest solving it?
q.a: By turning the video off and on again.

q.q: Why does he want a remote job?
q.a: He has worked from home for two years and would save almost two hours of commuting every day.

q.q: How does he stay in touch with his team?
q.a: A short video call every morning, a chat app for quick questions, and meeting colleagues once a month.

gaps.s: I think my ___ isn't working.
Don't worry, it happens all the ___.
I'd save almost two hours of ___ every day.

title: A competency-based question
lines: Can you give me an example of a time when you had to persuade someone who disagreed with you?
Certainly. In my previous role, our site manager wanted to postpone a safety inspection because we were behind schedule.

Strongly. We'd just modified the switchboard, and I wasn't comfortable energising it without testing. But rather than simply refusing, I tried to understand his concern, which was the penalty for late delivery.
So how did you approach it?
I proposed splitting the inspection. We tested the modified section that evening, outside working hours, and left the rest for the following week.
We found a loose connection that could have caused a serious fault. After that, he actually asked me to review the testing plan for the whole project.
What would you do differently, looking back?
I'd raise the issue earlier. If testing had been built into the schedule from the start, the conflict wouldn't have arisen at all.

q.q: Why did the site manager want to postpone the inspection?
q.a: Because they were behind schedule and he was worried about the penalty for late delivery.

q.q: How did the man solve the disagreement?
q.a: He proposed splitting the inspection and testing the modified section that evening, outside working hours.

q.q: What did the test reveal, and how did the manager react?
q.a: A loose connection that could have caused a serious fault; the manager then asked him to review the testing plan for the whole project.

q.q: What would he do differently now?
q.a: Raise the issue earlier so testing is built into the schedule from the start.

gaps.s: Our site manager wanted to ___ a safety inspection.
I wasn't comfortable ___ it without testing.
We found a ___ connection that could have caused a serious fault.

title: Panel interview: leadership
lines: You'd be managing a team of six, some of whom are older and more experienced than you. How would you handle that?
I think the key is not to pretend I know more than they do. I'd spend the first weeks listening, finding out what works and what frustrates them.
And if someone openly challenged your authority?
I'd talk to them privately rather than in front of the team. Often, resistance comes from feeling that their experience isn't being valued, so I'd try to give them real responsibility.
Then I'd be clear about expectations and the consequences of not meeting them. Being respectful doesn't mean avoiding difficult conversations.
Have you ever had to give negative feedback?

Yes, to a technician whose reports were consistently late. I focused on the impact, explaining that clients were complaining, rather than criticising him personally. It turned out he was struggling with the software, so we arranged some training.
So the problem wasn't really motivation.
Exactly. That's why I always try to understand the cause before jumping to conclusions.

q.q: What would the man do in his first weeks as manager?
q.a: Listen and find out what works and what frustrates the team.

q.q: How would he deal with someone who openly challenged his authority?
q.a: Talk to them privately and give them real responsibility; if that failed, be clear about expectations and consequences.

q.q: How did he give negative feedback to the technician?
q.a: He focused on the impact, explaining that clients were complaining, instead of criticising him personally.

q.q: What was the real cause of the problem?
q.a: The technician was struggling with the software, so they arranged training.

gaps.s: You'd be managing a team of six, some of whom are older and more ___ than you.
Being respectful doesn't mean avoiding difficult ___.
I always try to understand the cause before jumping to ___.

title: Feedback after a rejection
lines: Thanks for calling back. I was hoping to get some feedback on why I wasn't selected.
Of course. I should say first that it was a very close decision. Your technical answers were excellent.
That's good to hear. So what tipped the balance?
Honestly, the other candidate had more experience managing clients directly, and that's a big part of the role.
I see. I did mention my client work, but perhaps I didn't give enough detail.
That's fair. Your examples were mostly about technical problems. Next time, I'd include one about handling a difficult client.
That's really helpful. Was there anything else?
Just one small thing. Some of your answers were quite long. It's worth practising more concise versions.
I appreciate your honesty. Would you keep my CV in case something else comes up?
Definitely. In fact, we may be opening a design position in spring, which might suit you even better.

q.q: What did the interviewer say about the man's technical answers?
q.a: That they were excellent.

q.q: Why did the company choose the other candidate?
q.a: They had more experience managing clients directly, which is a big part of the role.

q.q: What two pieces of advice does she give him?
q.a: To include an example about handling a difficult client and to practise more concise answers.

q.q: What opportunity does she mention at the end?
q.a: A design position that may open in spring.

gaps.s: I should say first that it was a very ___ decision.
So what tipped the ___?
It's worth practising more ___ versions.

title: The curveball question
lines: Here's a slightly unusual question. If you joined us and found out after a month that a project you'd inherited was fundamentally flawed, what would you do?
I suppose the temptation would be to keep quiet, especially as the new person. But that would only postpone the problem and make it more expensive.
So you'd go straight to your manager?

Not immediately. First I'd want to be sure I wasn't missing something, so I'd quietly check my assumptions with whoever designed it. Coming in as the newcomer and declaring everything wrong is a fairly reliable way to lose allies.

Then I'd go to my manager with a clear account of the risk, an estimate of what it would cost to fix now versus later, and at least one realistic alternative. Bringing a problem without a proposal just shifts the burden.
What if your manager told you to carry on regardless?

That depends on the nature of the flaw. If it's a matter of efficiency, I'd put my concerns in writing and accept the decision. If it were a safety issue, frankly, I wouldn't sign it off, whatever the consequences for me.
On safety, I think it has to be. Everything else is negotiable.

q.q: Why does the man say keeping quiet would be a mistake?
q.a: It would only postpone the problem and make it more expensive.

q.q: What would he do before going to his manager, and why?
q.a: Check his assumptions with whoever designed it, because declaring everything wrong as a newcomer would make him lose allies.

q.q: What three things would he bring to his manager?
q.a: A clear account of the risk, an estimate of the cost of fixing it now versus later, and a realistic alternative.

q.q: How would his reaction differ between an efficiency problem and a safety problem?
q.a: For efficiency he'd put his concerns in writing and accept the decision; for safety he wouldn't sign it off.

gaps.s: A project you'd inherited was fundamentally ___.
Bringing a problem without a proposal just shifts the ___.
Everything else is ___.

title: Two offers on the table
lines: I'll be straightforward with you. I've received another offer, and I need to give them an answer by Friday.
I appreciate you telling us. May I ask what makes it attractive?
Partly the salary, which is around ten per cent higher. But mainly it's the chance to lead projects from the outset, rather than joining them halfway through.
I see. I can't promise to match the figure, but I can certainly go back to the director. As for leading projects, that's something we'd envisaged for the second year.
Could that be made more concrete? At the moment it's rather vague.
That's a reasonable request. We could put a review in writing at twelve months, specifically tied to taking over a project of your own.
That would go a long way. To be honest, I'd prefer to join you. The team impressed me, and your work in storage is exactly where I want to specialise.
Then let's try to make it work. I'll speak to the director this afternoon and come back to you by Thursday.
Thank you. I hope you don't feel I'm using the other offer as leverage.
Not at all. You've been open with us, which is exactly the attitude we're looking for.

q.q: What is the deadline for the other offer?
q.a: Friday.

q.q: What are the two attractions of the other offer?
q.a: A salary around ten per cent higher and, mainly, the chance to lead projects from the outset.

q.q: What does the woman propose to address his concern about leading projects?
q.a: A written review at twelve months tied to taking over a project of his own.

q.q: Why does the man prefer this company?
q.a: The team impressed him and their work in storage is where he wants to specialise.

gaps.s: Rather than joining them ___ through.
At the moment it's rather ___.
I hope you don't feel I'm using the other offer as ___.

title: Coaching session before a final interview
lines: Let's look at your answer about your biggest failure. You described it well, but you rushed through the part about what you learned.
I know. I suppose I'm uncomfortable dwelling on mistakes in an interview.
That's understandable, but it's precisely the part they're interested in. Anyone can describe a failure; what distinguishes candidates is the insight they draw from it.
So I should spend less time on the story itself?
Roughly a third on the situation, a third on what you did, and a third on what changed afterwards. And make the lesson specific. 'I learned to communicate better' is meaningless.
Fair enough. What I actually learned was to agree on acceptance criteria in writing before starting any design work.
Much better, because it's concrete and it shows you changed your practice. Now, the other thing is your body language. When you're unsure, you look down at the table.
I had no idea. I'll try to keep eye contact.
Don't overcorrect, though. Staring is just as off-putting. Glance away when you're thinking, then come back to them when you deliver the key point.
That's useful. It's strange how much of this has nothing to do with the actual job.
Interviews test whether you can do the job, but also whether people want to work with you. Both matter.

q.q: What was wrong with the man's answer about his biggest failure?
q.a: He rushed through the part about what he learned.

q.q: How does the woman suggest dividing the answer?
q.a: A third on the situation, a third on what he did, and a third on what changed afterwards.

q.q: What specific lesson did he actually learn?
q.a: To agree on acceptance criteria in writing before starting any design work.

q.q: What advice does she give about eye contact?
q.a: Not to overcorrect by staring; glance away when thinking and look back when delivering the key point.

gaps.s: I suppose I'm uncomfortable ___ on mistakes in an interview.
What distinguishes candidates is the ___ they draw from it.
Staring is just as ___.
